name: West Berawan
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Burkhardt, Jürgen M. 2014. The reconstruction of the phonology of Proto-Berawan. PhD thesis, Goethe Univ. Frankfurt (repository blocked); also Blust 1992, The long consonants of Long Terawan, BKI 148.

new_statements.quote: The nuclear syllable (S) is the ultimate syllable of the word. It is the only syllable in which all the vowel phonemes (except schwa) may occur and it is also the location of length contrasts in both vowels and consonants. [...] Stress in Berawan falls on the nuclear syllable (S). It is marked by length and by higher, often rising, pitch, and not by high average amplitude. The same pattern was also recognized in sentence utterances (see García-Bellido and Clayre 1997 §4.1.3. and Fig. 5b).
new_statements.citation: Clayre, Beatrice with Denny Belawing Wan. 1996. An introduction to Berawan phonology. The Sarawak Museum Journal L(71): 209-240. DOI 10.61507/smj22-1996-XLTF-14.
new_statements.locator: p. 212, section 2.0 'The Berawan Word' (PDF page 5 of the saved open preview)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed on the final (ultimate) syllable, which Clayre calls the nuclear syllable; it is the only syllable that carries the full vowel inventory and the vowel/consonant length contrasts. Stress is cued by length and by higher, often rising pitch rather than amplitude. Burkhardt 2006 (pp. 8, 15), from his own Long Terawan field data, confirms: stress 'always falls on the nucleus of the ultima', whether that nucleus is a short or long vowel, and is entirely predictable; the penultimate nucleus is always short.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in either Clayre & Wan 1996 (pp. 209-212 seen) or Burkhardt 2006. Words are maximally three syllables (usually disyllabic root + prefix).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Clayre & Wan note the analysis rests on one speaker and limited data and is preliminary, particularly regarding diphthongs; Burkhardt 2006 argues Clayre's nuclear-rhyme notion under-predicts stress in some vowel sequences and reanalyses them (e.g. /sapa:w/ 'roof', /mu.i/ 'wash') so that stress is uniformly on the ultima.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, from ~800 elicited words (citation forms) of one Long Terawan speaker analysed with CECIL; the authors state the same pattern was recognized in recorded sentences/frames but no detailed phrase-level study was made.
new_statements.identity_note: Both quoted sources describe the Long Terawan dialect (Tutoh River), which Kroeger's Sarawak classification and Glottolog equate with West Berawan west2564 (ISO zbw). Note Glottolog files Clayre & Wan 1996 under east2486 (East Berawan) and Burkhardt 2006/2008 under cent2098 (Central Berawan); both papers state explicitly that they describe Long Terawan, so they belong to west2564. Clayre & Wan's analysis rests on one speaker (Denny Belawing Wan, aged 34, Long Terawan).

sources.note: Sect. 5.1 'Word Stress and Clayre's notion of the nuclear rhyme', p. 8: 'Clayre (1996:212) states that stress in LTB falls on the ultimate syllable, an observation that I share.' Conclusion p. 15: 'The above generalization makes stress placement in LTB entirely predictable: it always falls on the nucleus of the ultima, which is either a short vowel (V) or a long one (V:).' Penultimate nucleus is always short (p. 9). Author's own field data from Long Terawan speakers.
